en: Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Having prostrated before the Lord and my gurus and ancestors, I now extract from the ocean of the Sāṃkhya scripture this treasury consisting of jewels of words, together with their meanings.
*Akāmyam*: Action performed without aiming for any fruit, whether visible or invisible, is called *akāmya*.
*Akkaḥ*: [A term for] a father-in-law.
The corner of the house. For example: "If one should find honey in the very hive, why should one go to the mountain?"
Aja means "birthless. In Sāṃkhya, the Puruṣa is called aja, and Prakṛti is called aja;
[the word] ajavat [is used] like aja.

Just as no sprout of the seed of instruction arose for King Aja, despite the teaching spoken by Vasiṣṭha, because his mind was stained by grief for his wife, even so, no sprout of the seed in the form of instruction arises in a mind stained by passion and other defilements.
The non-eternality of atoms:

there is no eternality for the atoms of earth and the other elements, because those atoms are also heard in scripture to be effects. Although the scriptural passage making known that atoms are effects is not perceived due to the loss of time, it can nevertheless be inferred from the words of the Teacher and from Smṛti. Thus says Manu: "The minute, perishable particles (mātrās) of the five [elements] which are recorded—along with these, all this comes into being in successive order. And regarding this, the Cakṣuṣa says:

The Sāṃkhya tenet is that the sense organs possess the capacity to illuminate what they reach. In this position, one need not raise the objection that the eye must be admitted as consisting of light (*taijasa*) because it is only light that is seen to travel rapidly to very distant places in the form of rays; for even if it were not composed of light, its reaching to very distant places would be possible through a specific modification of its function (*vṛtti*), just as in the case of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).

Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*), without abandoning the body, moves outward from the tip of the nose to a certain distance by means of its function known as *prāṇana*, so too the eye, though not composed of light (*ataijasam*), would instantly move toward the sun and other objects by means of a specific modification of its function known as *ālocana* (perception).

The ultimate human goal (*atyantapuruṣārtha*) is precisely the absolute cessation of the three kinds of suffering—those pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), those pertaining to external beings (*ādhibhautika*), and those pertaining to divine or supernatural forces (*ādhidaivika*). Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya-sūtra states: "Now, the ultimate human goal is the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering."

However, by the term *puruṣārtha* alone, there is an understanding of both enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*). Thus, the teacher Gauḍapāda says: "The purpose of the *puruṣa* is twofold: characterized by the perception of sound and so forth, and characterized by the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. The perception of sound and so forth is the attainment of enjoyments such as fragrance in the worlds beginning with Brahma; the perception of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* is liberation."

Now, regarding the word *atha*: the mention of the word *atha* at the beginning of a treatise (*śāstra*) is for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). For example, in the passage: "Now, the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering is the supreme human goal."
Independence from the unseen (adṛṣṭanairapekṣyam):

For the unseen is indeed the effect of the intellect; therefore, while it may serve as an auxiliary to the Great Principle (mahat) and the others in the production of the ego (ahaṅkāra) and so forth, nevertheless, in the case of primordial nature (prakṛti) performing its own specific effects, there is no assistance provided by the unseen; rather, non-discrimination (aviveka) alone serves as the auxiliary.
Non-contradiction with the Śruti on Non-duality:

Even if duality exists according to the Sāṃkhya system, there is no contradiction with the Śruti on non-duality; for in some instances, the Śruti teaches non-duality solely for the sake of generating dispassion in those possessed of passion toward things other than the Puruṣa. Thus, the Sāṃkhya-sūtra states: "There is no contradiction with the Śruti, because that [non-duality] is established for the sake of producing dispassion in those possessed of passion. This is not unrighteousness (adharma).
It is the effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of *rajas* and *tamas*.

Regarding the qualified aspirants—there are three types of those qualified for knowledge: superior, intermediate, and inferior. That is to say, for the superior qualified aspirants, liberation is accomplished through hearing alone; for the intermediate qualified aspirants, through both hearing and reflection; and for the inferior qualified aspirants, liberation is accomplished through all three—hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). Therefore, it was solely due to the defect of being dull-witted that Virocana and others did not develop the knowledge capable of dissolving the mind through hearing alone; it is not that hearing lacks the capacity to generate knowledge.

Thus, although liberation is established for the highest qualified seeker through mere hearing (*śravaṇa*) alone, both reflection (*manana*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are also prescribed for the sake of firmness.

*Adhyavasāya*—the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) known as determination—is as follows: every agent, having first perceived objects through the senses, reflected upon them with the mind, and identified with them through the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) thinking "I am authorized in this," determines "this must be done by me," and subsequently proceeds to act. Among these stages, that which is the firm conviction "this is to be done" is *adhyavasāya*; it is the unique function of the intellect (*buddhi*).
And it is said in the *Yuktidīpikā*:

"What is this determination (*adhyavasāya*)? That cognition which is a certainty, the grasping of an object, such as 'this is indeed a cow' or 'this is indeed a person,' that is determination. Furthermore, Vijñānabhikṣu maintains that determination is synonymous with certainty (*niścaya*).
Superimposition (*adhyāsa*)—

Metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is superimposition (*āropa*). Just as victory and defeat, which actually belong to the warriors, are metaphorically attributed to the king, so too the quality of being a creator and so forth, which resides in *prakṛti*, is metaphorically attributed to the *puruṣas*. This very process is superimposition (*adhyāsa*). Or, for example, it is like the cognition "this is silver" arising from the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl. Non-authoritativeness characterized by non-performance:
when the performance of a Vedic meaning is impossible, there arises non-authoritativeness characterized by non-performance regarding that Veda which propounds such a meaning.

"Beginningless" (anādi) means devoid of a beginning. It is of two kinds: partless beginninglessness (akhaṇḍānādi) and continuous beginninglessness (pravāhānādi). Partless beginninglessness refers to the Self (ātman), while continuous beginninglessness refers to non-discrimination (aviveka). "Non-return" (anāvṛtti):
Liberation (*apavarga*). According to the Vedic scripture, "He does not return again," [there is no rebirth].
The theory of indeterminate manifestation (*anirvacanīya-khyāti*):

This refers to a manifestation of the world that is distinct from both the real (*sat*) and the unreal (*asat*), and therefore incapable of being defined either as existent or non-existent. Such a manifestation is called *anirvacanīya-khyāti*. However, this too is not accepted by the Sāṃkhya school, because an entity distinct from both the real and the unreal is unestablished; for conceptualization is appropriate only in accordance with what is observed in experience.

Inference (*anumāna*) is the knowledge of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) arising from the perception of the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—that is, a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) having the form of the pervader. Alternatively, inference is preceded by the mark (*liṅga*) and the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*). The mark is the pervaded; the possessor of the mark is the pervader. The pervaded is that which is invariably connected to the true nature of the object through the removal of suspected or superimposed limiting conditions (*upādhi*); that to which it is so connected is the pervader.

The term *liṅgi-pada* should be repeated twice here; by this, the cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*)—in the sense that "this has a mark" (*liṅgam asyāsti*)—is also shown. Thus, Vācaspatimiśra maintains that inference is preceded by the cognition of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) and the cognition of the property of the subject. However, the teacher Gauḍapāda states that inference is preceded by the mark (*liṅgapūrvaka*), wherein the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is inferred by means of the mark, just as a mendicant is inferred by means of his staff.

And [inference] preceded by the mark (*liṅga*) is that where the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*) is inferred from the mark; for example, having seen an ascetic, one thinks, "This is his triple staff. Bhāvagaṇeśa says it is a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*) in the form of the subject (*pakṣa*) qualified by the probandum (*sādhya*), which arises from the cognition of the mark.
Inference (*anumiti*) is the valid cognition (*pramiti*) produced by inference—that is to say, the human awareness resulting therefrom.
Internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—
the triad consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) is the internal organ.
Misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

When one object appears in the form of another, this is precisely what is called *anyathākhyāti* (misapprehension through transformation). This too is not accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, because it involves the fallacy of self-contradiction in their own statement. For when the silver appearing in a mother-of-pearl shell is expressed by the word "otherwise" (*anyathā*), that silver exists as non-existent, being comparable to a man’s horn. Thus, there would be a contradiction in their own words: "that which is non-existent appears. Therefore, even *anyathākhyāti* is not worthy of acceptance. Regarding the phrase "the qualities have the activity of mutual production": it means that the *guṇas* produce and, in other words, transform one another. And in this context, that transformation of the *guṇas* takes a similar form.
They function as mutual pairs—
meaning the *guṇas* exist as companions to one another, that is to say, they function through inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
They function as mutual subduers—

For the qualities (guṇas), by virtue of their specific purposes, manifest spontaneously and mutually suppress one another. Therefore, when *sattva* manifests, it suppresses *rajas* and *tamas*, attaining a peaceful state (*śāntā vṛtti*). Likewise, *rajas* suppresses *sattva* and *tamas*, attaining a terrible state (*ghorā vṛtti*), and *tamas* suppresses *sattva* and *rajas*, regaining its own deluded state (*mūḍhā vṛtti*).
Their activities are based on mutual dependence.

Just as three staffs, by supporting one another, perform the function of holding up a pot, so too the three *guṇas*, by depending on one another, perform their respective functions in the form of illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and restraint (*niyamana*).
Regarding this, there is a traditional scripture (*āgama*): "They are all mutual companions; they all go everywhere."
Sattva is the mate of rajas, and rajas is the mate of sattva.
In the pair consisting of tamas, both sattva and rajas are also present;
the pair of both sattva and tamas is called tamas.
"Neither their beginning, nor their conjunction, nor their disjunction is perceived.
Regarding liberation (*apavarga*):

it is the indifference of either of the two—the *prakṛti* or the *puruṣa*—or of the Self. The indifference of *prakṛti* is its non-engagement toward one who possesses discriminative knowledge. The indifference of the *puruṣa* is his lack of attachment to *prakṛti*.
Non-authorship (*apauruṣeyatvam*):

Whether an object be perceived or unperceived, that object regarding which the cognition "this was made" arises is considered authored (*pauruṣeya*). However, according to the Sāṃkhya school, authorship does not consist merely in being uttered by a person; for if that were the case, even the Vedas would incur the status of being authored, since they too were uttered by the Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣa*). Non-external perception (*abāhyapratyakṣam*): [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text].
Perception distinct from sensory perception;
activity—
every operation.
Adherence (*abhiniveśa*) is the fear of death and so forth, consisting of such thoughts as "May I not cease to be" or "May I continue to exist. Arrogance (*abhimāna*)—

Vijñānabhikṣu maintains that *ahaṅkāra* (ego) has *buddhi* (intellect) as its material cause and is a specific substance (*dravyaviśeṣa*) in the form of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). As it has been said: "The internal organ is indeed one; like a seed, a sprout, and a tree, it assumes the state of being both effect and instrument due solely to the difference in its three stages. For this very reason, in the passage "Mind, the Great One, Intellect, Brahma, Fortitude, Consciousness, and the Lord," mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*) are stated to be synonyms.

Manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is the appearance from their cause of things such as jars and cloths that already exist therein, just as the manifestation of oil occurs within sesame seeds where it already exists.

Non-deceptiveness (*amāyikatva*) means truthfulness, stability, or being uncreated. Because the Self (*ātman*) is truthful, stable, and uncreated, it is non-deceptive. Dream-objects are deceptive in comparison to waking objects; however, in relation to the Self, even waking objects are indeed deceptive. [The] parts—

The five members of a syllogism (*nyāya*) are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). Among these, the statement of the thing to be proven is the proposition, such as "sound is impermanent. The reason is that which establishes the thing to be proven through similarity with the example, such as "because it has the property of being produced. This means that something having the property of being produced is seen to be impermanent. Likewise, [it is established] through dissimilarity—that is, by way of dissimilarity with the example—the reason is that which establishes the thing to be proven.

For example: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; for that which has the property of not being produced is seen to be permanent, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth."

An example (*udāharaṇa*) is an instance that, by virtue of sharing the properties of the probandum (*sādhyasādharmya*), possesses those same properties (*taddharmabhāvī*). For instance, when proving the impermanence of sound by means of the reason "possessing an origin," an example such as a jar is given, as in: "like a jar. This is a positive (*anvayī*) example.

An example by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) also exists. Thus, the *Nyāya-sūtra* states: "Or, from the opposite of that, the reverse [is established]. That is to say, an example which possesses the property of not being that [subject] due to its dissimilarity with the probandum (*sādhyavaidharmya*) is also an illustration (*udāharaṇa*). For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it has the property of being produced; whatever does not have the property of being produced is permanent, such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth. Application (*upanaya*) is the application of the probandum based on the example, either as "so it is" (*tathā*) or "not so it is" (*na tathā*).

Just as in the example, a jar or similar object is seen to be impermanent because it possesses the property of origination, so too sound possesses the property of origination—this statement is the application (*upanaya*).

The restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the presentation of the reason (*hetu*) is the conclusion (*nigamana*); for example, "Therefore, sound is impermanent because it possesses the property of origination"—this statement is the conclusion. These definitions of the proposition and the other members are accepted here in this treatise exactly as they are in the *Nyāyadarśana*.
Ignorance (*avidyā*)—

The classification of error (*viparyaya-bheda*). It consists in the cognition of the permanent in the impermanent, the pure in the impure, happiness in suffering, and the self in the non-self. Thus says the *Yogasūtra*: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the permanent, the pure, the happy, and the self in that which is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self; it is non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the conceit of non-difference. This includes the conceit of the self in the body, senses, and so forth, or the conceit of non-difference between the self and the body, senses, etc., as well as the conceit of the attributes of the body and so forth [belonging to the self]. Regarding this, the *Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya* states: "Non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of discrimination, and it is an attribute of the intellect (*buddhi*)."

The *aviśeṣas* (non-specifics) are the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), the five *tanmātras*. They are called *aviśeṣa* because, according to the etymology, there is no "specificity" (*viśeṣa*)—in the form of being peaceful, terrible, or delusive—within them. "The *tanmātras* are the non-specifics," states the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*.
This is the theory of the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*).

The manifestation of things that are absolutely non-existent is "unreal manifestation" (asatkhyāti). And this is not what is intended by the Sāṃkhyas, like the manifestation of a man's horn and so forth.
Egoism (asmitā) is the notion of identity between the self and the non-self, consisting in the form: "there is no self distinct from the body and so forth."

Incapacity (*aśakti*) consists of twenty-eight varieties. These are the seventeen types of impairment of the intellect (*buddhi*), together with the eleven types of impairment of the sense organs. Among these, there are seventeen inherent impairments of the intellect resulting from the opposites of the nine types of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and the eight types of attainment (*siddhi*). Furthermore, there are eleven impairments of the intellect caused by the incapacity of the eleven sense organs. Thus, when combined, incapacity is of twenty-eight kinds.

And so it is stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "The eleven defects of the sense organs, together with the defects of the intellect, are designated as incapacity; there are seventeen defects of the intellect resulting from the inversion of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and perfection (*siddhi*). [Thus ends the discussion of] the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).

It has the function of self-conceit (*abhimāna*). The general definition of *ahaṅkāra* (the ego-principle) is precisely this self-conceit in the form of "I. It is threefold: 1. The *vaikṛta* (modified), which is dominated by *sattva*, is the cause of the sense organs. 2. The *bhūtādi* (source of elements), which is dominated by *tamas*, is the cause of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*). 3. The *taijasa* (fiery), which is dominated by *rajas*, is the cause of both. As it is stated in the *Yuktidīpikā*: "From this Great Self (*mahat*), these three selves—characterized as *ahaṅkāra*—are produced: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*. It is like a snake shedding its skin.

Just as a snake effortlessly casts off its worn-out skin with the intention of discarding it, even so should the seeker of liberation cast off primordial nature (prakṛti), which has been experienced since beginningless time and is now worn out, with the intention of discarding it.
[The subtle body (ātivāhika-śarīra)—]

Vijñānabhikṣu maintains that there is another subtle body, material and distinct from the *liṅgaśarīra*, called the *ātivāhikaśarīra*. It is termed *ātivāhika* because it carries the *liṅgadeha* from one world to another. Since the movement of the *liṅgaśarīra* is impossible without a support of material elements—just as a painting cannot move independently—the *liṅgaśarīra* exists as a separate entity by virtue of being the locus of experience or the locus for the reflection of the *puruṣa*.

The proof for this is found in scripture and tradition: "A person the size of a thumb, the inner self, is always seated in the hearts of men," and "Yama forcibly dragged out the person the size of a thumb. These are the Śruti and Smṛti.

The teacher Aniruddha, however, states that the subtle body (*sūkṣma-śarīra*) itself is the *ativāhika* (conveying) body, and not some other distinct body. Regarding non-duality (*ātmadvaita*): the Vedāntins maintain that non-duality consists in the absolute lack of difference between the selves and the manifold of objects of experience, as well as among the selves themselves. This is not accepted by the Sāṃkhyas, because difference is established by the very marks found in the passage "the one unborn" (*ajāmekām*), such as the abandonment or non-abandonment of *prakṛti*. Furthermore, those statements of non-difference that are observed serve to indicate equality, as they form a single syntactical unit with Vedic texts that establish equality, such as "the stainless one attains equality" (*nirañjanaḥ sāmyamupaiti*).

The mutual difference among selves is established by the specific determination of birth, death, and instruments, as well as by their non-simultaneous activity; furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning non-difference refer to the genus (jāti). Thus, even due to the sublation by perception which apprehends difference, there is no non-duality of the self.
The Self is partless (*niravayava*).

According to the authority of the scripture, "Partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless," the Self is indeed partless. As for scriptural passages such as, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā; by its [the Lord's] constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded," these indicate a relationship of part and whole merely through non-distinction (*avibhāga*), like that between space and water, but not by virtue of having actual parts.
The Self exists.

The person (puruṣa) is indeed established in a general sense as the object of the cognition "I know. Furthermore, he exists as distinct from the body and so forth, due to the difference in nature between being subject to transformation and being unchanging. Nature (prakṛti) and the rest are established as undergoing transformation through perception, inference, and scripture; however, the person is inferred to be unchanging because his objects are always known [by him]. For instance, just as the eye has only color-and-form as its object and not taste or other qualities, even when the conditions for contact are equal, so too for the person, it is only the modification of his own intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) that becomes the object.

It is not the case that another object is postulated merely because of the similarity in its contact [with the senses], for such a distinction is inferred from the force of the resulting experience. Rather, an object becomes an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) only by being mounted upon a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), and not by itself, since otherwise the consequence would be the perception of everything at all times. Furthermore, those modifications of the intellect do not remain unknown; for if one were to admit the existence of knowledge, pleasure, desire, and so forth while they remain unperceived, then just as with jars and other objects, there would arise doubts regarding them as well, in the form: "Do I know or not? Am I happy or not? and so on.

Therefore, because those [mental modifications] are always known, it follows that their seer is the conscious one, who is unchanging. If the conscious one were subject to change, there would sometimes be a modification into blindness; consequently, even when a mental modification exists, its non-perception could lead to the occurrence of doubt and other such states. Furthermore, from the use of the genitive case in expressions such as "this body is mine" and "this intellect is mine," it is established that the Self exists as distinct from the body and other such things.
Regarding the *ādhidaivika* (divine): *ādhidaivika* suffering is that which proceeds with reference to the gods, such as fire, wind, and so forth.

*Ādhibhautika*—suffering pertaining to living beings (*ādhibhautika*) is that which arises with reference to beings such as humans, cattle, birds, and so forth. *Ādhyātmika*—suffering pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*) is that which arises with reference to the body and the mind, upon which the notion of "self" is superimposed. *Ānumānika*—that which is established through inference, such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest.

*Ānuśravika* refers to the collection of Vedic rituals. It is called *anuśrava* because it is heard following the recitation of a teacher; that is to say, it is merely heard and not created by anyone. That which exists in this *anuśrava* (the Veda) is *ānuśravika*, meaning that which is obtained or known therein.

Manifestation (*āvirbhāva*)—the appearance or becoming evident of that which exists even previously, as if it were only after the operation of a cause; for example, the manifestation of oil existing in sesame seeds, or the manifestation of milk existing in *saurabheyī* cows.
Sitting (*āsana*).
That which, being stable, serves as a means to happiness—such as the Svastika and other postures—is *āsana*. Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "Posture is that which is steady and comfortable.
Āsuri was a disciple of Kapila. The authority for this is: "This supreme purifier the Sage imparted to Āsuri out of compassion."

The sense organ (*indriya*)—the nature of being a sense organ consists in having the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as its material cause. Among these, there are five organs of cognition (*jñānendriya*), known as the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and skin; and five organs of action (*karmendriya*), known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Including the mind (*manas*), which partakes of the nature of both, there are eleven sense organs. Furthermore, the sense organs themselves are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*); however, for those who are deluded, the cognition of the sense organs occurs with respect to their physical seats (*golakādi*), which serve as their substrates.

If the sense organ were merely the physical ball (golaka) and so forth, then hearing would be impossible for one whose ears are severed, and there would be the undesirable consequence of a person with cataracts perceiving color. Furthermore, due to the difference in their capacities, the sense organs are manifold; they are not a single sense organ.
[This concludes the discussion on] the non-material nature of the sense organs.

In the Sāṃkhya system, because the sense organs arise from the principle of *ahaṅkāra*, they possess the nature of being derived from *ahaṅkāra* (*āhaṅkārika*), but not the nature of being material (*bhautika*). Therefore, the view that the sense organs are material is refuted by the Nyāya school. Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya Sūtra states: "The sense organs do not have the elements as their material cause, because of the scriptural testimony regarding their derivation from *ahaṅkāra*. And the scripture says: "From this [the Unmanifest] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs; as well as space, air, fire, water, and the earth which supports the universe. This is like the case of the arrow-maker.

Just as the one-pointedness of mind of an archer who is creating an arrow of reeds is not lost even while a king passes by his side, in the same way, there is no loss of meditative absorption for the yogin whose mind is one-pointed. The Lord said:

He is accepted as the creator of the world and is agreed upon by the Nyāya and other schools. Regarding this, some say: "In the Sāṃkhya system, there is no Lord; therefore, the Sāṃkhya philosophy is 'without a Lord' (nirīśvara). For this very reason, the Sāṃkhya-sūtras state: "The Lord is not established [as a cause], because neither the liberated nor the bound exist [independently of Him]; thus His existence is not proven. In either case, He would be ineffective; [His existence is asserted] only as praise for the liberated soul or for one perfected through meditation. This is the intended meaning: [The opponent's argument is: If the Lord were the cause of the world, He would have to be either liberated or bound. If He were liberated, He would lack the capacity to act, as a liberated being is free from all effort. If He were bound, He would be subject to suffering and thus incapable of creating the world. Furthermore, since there is no third state between these two, the existence of a Lord cannot be established. Therefore, the Sāṃkhya system maintains that the world arises solely from the evolution of primordial matter (prakṛti), without the intervention of a divine creator.

In the context of defining the characteristics of perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa-nirūpaṇa*), having resolved the suspicion of the definition’s lack of pervasiveness (*lakṣaṇāvyāpti*) regarding the non-external perception of yogis—by means of two sūtras stating, "There is no fault because the perception of yogis is not non-external," or "There is no fault because of the connection with the attainment of excellence over latent objects"—he now refutes that very same suspicion of the definition’s lack of pervasiveness even regarding the perception of Īśvara, by way of demonstrating the non-establishment of Īśvara, through the four sūtras beginning with "Because Īśvara is unestablished" (*īśvarāsiddheḥ*).

The meaning is that God himself does not exist; how then could there be any suspicion regarding the definition, pervasion (*vyāpti*), or its refutation in relation to His perception? This very interpretation is shared by commentators such as Aniruddha and others.

The Vijñāna-bhikṣus, however, analyze [the matter] as follows: "The intention of the author of the Sūtras is not refuted by these sūtras regarding Īśvara. If that were the case, he would have composed the sūtra simply as 'due to the non-existence of Īśvara' (*īśvarābhāvāt*), rather than formulating the sūtra in the form 'because of the non-establishment of Īśvara' (*īśvarāsiddheḥ*). Thus, Īśvara is not established as the creator of the world, because the agency of creation belongs to Prakṛti alone; Īśvara possesses only the status of being the presiding controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of Prakṛti. And this has been explained in detail in the *Brahmasūtra-vijñānāmṛta-bhāṣya*."

This has also been clarified in the commentary on the Sāṃkhya-pravacana-bhāṣya in the sūtra-commentary: "The state of being a presiding controller [of nature] is due to its proximity, like a magnet. Therefore, those [commentators] have explained the aforementioned four sūtras solely as having the purpose of negating the agency of creating the world preceded by volition (saṅkalpa).

Although the resolution of the doubt regarding the non-pervasion of the definition in the case of the perception of God (Īśvara) arises precisely through the resolution of the perception of yogis, nevertheless, because of the contextual connection (*prasaṅga-saṅgati*) consisting in the fact that [the definition] must not be neglected when it has been recalled, the intention of the Sāṃkhyas—namely, the denial of God’s status as the creator of the world—is introduced here by way of that very context; such is their view.
