The intended meaning of these sūtras is precisely the negation of the existence of God (*īśvara*). Otherwise, if the Sāṃkhya tradition were to maintain that "God exists" as a reality, then the doubt regarding the perception of God would already be resolved by the very resolution of the perception of the yogin; consequently, these sūtras would be purposeless and irrelevant. For this is not a discussion concerning the agency of creation, but rather a discussion concerning the definition of perception.

The Vijñānabhikṣu also, in the commentary on the third chapter of the Sūtra, stating that "the proof of such an Īśvara is established," asserts the proof of a produced (janya) Īśvara who is merged in primordial nature (prakṛti), thereby accepting that the eternal (nitya) Īśvara is the subject of dispute.
Likewise, the author of the Māṭhara-vṛtti also says:

Why is God not the cause? Because He is devoid of attributes (*nirguṇatvāt*). These creatures possess attributes; the three attributes—sattva, rajas, and tamas—are present within these creatures. Observing these attributes, we conclude: "These creatures have arisen from Nature (*prakṛti*). If God were the cause, then from a God who is devoid of attributes, the creatures would likewise be devoid of attributes. But this is not the case; therefore, God is not the cause.

In reality, however, there are two streams of Sāṃkhya inquiry flowing: the theistic Sāṃkhya stream and the atheistic Sāṃkhya stream. Vijñānabhikṣu also accepts this; for this very reason, he states in his *Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya*: "And this refutation of God is [presented] as a bold assertion (*prauḍhi-vāda*) by those who hold to a single position."

Just as within the single Buddhist system there are four well-known streams, within the single system of Gautama there are two—the Navya and Prācya—and within the single system of Vyāsa there are numerous schools; so too, although the Sāṃkhya system possesses two streams, the theistic (Seśvara) and the atheistic (Nirīśvara), it is the theistic stream alone that is more appealing. Even when a negation is observed in some places, it is appropriate to understand it as being directed against the agency of God, and not against the very nature of God himself.

For instance: it is established by the authority of the Sūtra, "Even though [the Self] is not an agent, its association with agency exists due to dependence," that Nature (prakṛti) is the agent while being dependent on another. And that "other" is the Self alone, not the Lord (Īśvara) as accepted in Nyāya. Consequently, because of being reflected in Nature, the conceit of omniscience and omnipotence resides in the Self, but it is not real. Thus says the Sūtra: "For He is all-knowing and the doer of all."

In this Sūtra, the author of the Vṛttisāra has interpreted the word "sahi" as meaning "the very primordial nature" (prakṛti). If there were such a self as we maintain—one possessing the aforementioned conceit—then let that be God. However, there is no proof for a God as conceived by the Naiyāyikas. That is to say, the Sāṃkhyas deny only an agent as God, but not a self who possesses the conceit of agency and so forth as being God.

For this very reason, the author of the *Vṛtti* established in his commentary on the Sūtra that the Self (*ātman*) is twofold—namely, the higher (*para*) and the lower (*apara*)—in the passage: "The purpose of Pradhāna is for its own sake or for the sake of liberation from bondage.
This refers to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

The world cannot have the Self alone as its material cause (*upādāna*), nor can it be ignorance (*avidyā*) residing in the Self, nor is it possible for both the Self and ignorance combined—like two potsherds—to be the material cause of the world, because the Self is unattached (*asaṅga*). For it is only through that specific kind of conjunction called "attachment" (*saṅga*) that the transformation of substances occurs. Therefore, due to this lack of attachment, the non-dual Self alone cannot be the material cause. Nor can it be so even by means of ignorance, because its connection with ignorance is also ruled out by its very nature of being unattached. Just like the impossibility of each being a material cause individually, the possibility of their combination as a material cause is also impossible precisely because of the lack of attachment.

Suitability for being the material cause (*upādāna-yogyatā*) consists in possessing qualities (*guṇavattva*) and being adhesive (*saṅgitva*). Due to the absence of these two, the *puruṣa*, despite its eternity, is not the material cause. Furthermore, since the principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) are themselves of the nature of effects, they too are not the material cause of the world. Therefore, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone is the material cause of the world. This is like the non-establishment of an object of meditation (*upāsyāsiddhi-vat*).

Just as those such as Brahmā, who are objects of worship, do not possess the state of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) despite their possession of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), because it is heard that even they engage in the practice of yoga during the "yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*) and other states; likewise, even in the possession of sovereign power (*aiśvaryayoga*), there is no state of having accomplished all that was to be done, because it is followed by decay, excess, and suffering.
The "organ of both" is the mind (*manas*), because it is the activator of both the organs of cognition and the organs of action—just like a camel carrying saffron.

Just as a camel’s carrying of saffron is for the sake of its owner, so too the creation produced by the Pradhāna is solely for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the Puruṣa. Regarding the "single-elemental" view: others hold that the body consists of earth alone, while the other elements serve merely as supports. It is only because the other elements act as supports that the body is designated as being composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*). This is the position held by the Siddhāntins. Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya-sūtra states: "The body is not composed of the five elements."
Sovereignty is a quality of the intellect (buddhi), from which the manifestation of the powers such as atomization (aṇimā) arises.
Indifference—
Non-agency is neutrality.

Kapila is the founder of the Sāṃkhya system; as it is said in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "He who, in the beginning, sustains with his knowledges the seer Kapila when he is born, and beholds him as he is being born."

"Kapila, the supreme seer, is called the proponent of Sāṃkhya" (Mahābhārata); "The fifth [incarnation], named Kapila, the Lord of Siddhas, proclaimed to Āsuri the Sāṃkhya, which determines the collection of principles, as it had been obscured by time" (Śrīmad Bhāgavata); "Kapila was the son of Brahmā" (Sāṃkhyakārikā with Gauḍapāda’s Bhāṣya).

The incarnation of Viṣṇu was born from the great sage Kardama upon Devahūtī, the daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu; as stated in the Śrīmad Bhāgavata: "After a long time had passed, the Blessed Lord Madhusūdana entered the seed of Kardama and was born from her like fire from wood. O increaser of your fame, he shall become known in the world by the name Kapila; he is the sovereign lord of the hosts of Siddhas and is highly esteemed by the teachers of Sāṃkhya."

Regarding the *Mahābhārata*’s statement that Kapila was an incarnation of Agni— namely, "The great seer whom ascetics always call Kapila is indeed Agni himself, known by the name Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya and Yoga"— the venerable Udayavīra Śāstrin maintains that to accept this as implying a duality or even a triad of Kapilas is nothing but an error.

Accordingly, even according to the *Mahābhārata*, Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, was indeed an incarnation of Viṣṇu; however, because he reduced the sons of Sagara to ashes with the fire of his wrath, his nature as "fire" became well-known. Vijñānabhikṣu also refutes the duality of Kapilas. [The instrument] is of thirteen kinds: the internal organ is threefold, consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*); and the external is tenfold, consisting of the organs of perception and the organs of action.

The function of the instruments (*karaṇa*) consists of that which is to be brought forth (*āhārya*), that which is to be pervaded (*vyāpya*), that which is to be sustained (*dhārya*), that which is to be sustained by others (*dhārayitavya*), that which is to be manifested (*prakāśya*), and that which is to be manifested by others (*prakāśayitavya*). For example, for the organs of action (*karmendriya*), speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are their respective objects to be pervaded. By means of the activity (*vṛtti*) characterized as *prāṇa* and so forth, the body is to be sustained by the three internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Likewise, for the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*), sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects to be manifested. There is a lack of common locus (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) between the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) and the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*).

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose function is self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and that alone is the possessor of volitional activity (*kṛtimān*). This is because activity is generally observed to follow immediately after self-conceit. However, the *puruṣa* is not the possessor of volitional activity, because it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). Thus, although the ego is the agent, the experience of enjoyment (*bhoga*) ultimately culminates in consciousness (*cit*) alone. Nor should it be argued that if enjoyment resulted from an action residing in one thing while occurring in another, there would be no rule regarding which specific *puruṣa* experiences it; for the enjoyment belongs to that consciousness with which the action has been associated by the ego, since the enjoyment is produced by that very action.

And thus, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) which, taking up a particular person, produces the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of "I" and "mine" with respect to an insentient object—the activity of that ego-sense is said to belong to that self (*ātman*). And by that very activity, experience (*bhoga*) is acquired for that self; therefore, there is no inconsistency regarding the restriction of experience to specific persons.
The organs of action (*karmendriya*) are five: speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the generative organ.
*Kāmya* is action performed with a desire for its fruit.

*Kāla* (time) is twofold: eternal (*nitya*) and fragmentary (*khaṇḍa*). Among these, eternal time is simply a specific quality of *prakṛti*, whereas fragmentary time arises from space (*ākāśa*) through conjunction with various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Like the action of time and so forth: just as one season passes and another proceeds, and such actions of time and the like occur by themselves, in exactly the same way, the activity of the Pradhāna will also occur by itself.

Like the conch of a young girl: just as a jingling sound arises from the mutual contact of the finger-tips of a young girl’s hands, so too, through contact with many, quarrels arise from the production of passion, hatred, and the like; therefore, one should not associate with many.
Like a woman of good family (*kulavadhū*):

just as a woman of good family, feeling ashamed because her husband has perceived a fault in her—as determined by the thought "my husband has seen my fault"—does not approach her husband; in the same way, *prakṛti* also becomes ashamed due to the perception of faults such as its being subject to transformation and its nature consisting of suffering by the *puruṣa*, and thus does not approach the *puruṣa* again.
Kevalajñāna (isolated knowledge).

Pure knowledge is that which is free from the defects of error. Its essential nature is expressed as: "I am not, nothing is mine, I do not exist. In this regard, by the first [statement], the agency of the self is negated; by the second, attachment is negated; and by the third, identity is negated. Kaivalya is the absolute absence of the threefold suffering; that is kaivalya.

Like a silkworm: just as a silkworm, which is a specific kind of insect, binds itself with its own produced cocoon, even so does *prakṛti* bind itself through seven forms—dharma, adharma, dispassion, passion, power, lack of power, and ignorance—which are causes of suffering. Furthermore, it liberates itself from suffering by means of the single form consisting of knowledge.
Like milk: [as milk transforms into curds].

Just as milk transforms by itself into the form of curd independently of human effort, so too does the transformation of the *pradhāna* into the form of the *mahat* and other principles occur even for that which is insentient, without the exertion of another.
The *guṇas* are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

*Sattva* is light, illuminating, and of the nature of pleasure. Among these, its lightness is the opposite of heaviness; it is because of this that fire flames upward, wind moves horizontally, and the sense organs possess proficiency in their respective functions. *Sattva* is also illuminating, for it is through it that the sense organs manifest objects. *Rajas* is of the nature of pain, mobile, and the stimulator (exciter) of *sattva* and *tamas*; therefore, it is the cause of activity.
*Tamas* consists of delusion (*moha*); it is heavy and obscuring. For this very reason, it acts as a regulator of all things.

Like the spinning of a wheel—just as a potter’s wheel continues to spin for some time by its own momentum even after the potter’s action has ceased, so too, even though no new karma arises after the dawn of knowledge (*jñāna*), the *jīvanmukta* remains, maintaining the body which continues to act through the momentum of previously begun karma (*prārabdha-karma*).

*Cāturbhautikaḥ* (composed of the four elements): Intending that space (*ākāśa*) is not a productive cause, some maintain that the body is the transformation of only the four elements, excluding space.

*Cicchāyāpattiḥ* (the falling of the shadow of consciousness): Just as the reflection of a face appears in a mirror, that reflection of consciousness which is postulated in the intellect (*buddhi*) for the purpose of perceiving consciousness is called *cicchāyāpatti*. It is also termed *caitanyādhyāsa* (superimposition of consciousness) and *cidāveśa* (pervasion by consciousness).
"Citta" refers to either the intellect (*buddhi*) or the great principle (*mahattattva*).

"The self whose nature is consciousness" means that the self is indeed of the nature of consciousness alone, and not of the dual nature of both bliss and consciousness. This is because a single substratum cannot possess two distinct natures such as bliss and consciousness simultaneously; for instance, at the time of experiencing pain or knowledge, pleasure is not perceived, which demonstrates the difference between knowledge and pleasure. Nor can it be said that pleasure is merely a subordinate variety of knowledge itself, because the knowledge that constitutes the very nature of the self is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*).

Nor should it be argued that the Self possesses both the nature of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*) solely on the strength of the scriptural text, "Brahman is truth, consciousness, and bliss" (*satyaṃ vijñānamānandaṃ brahma*). This is because the absence of bliss is also established by such scriptural passages as, "Neither bliss nor devoid of bliss," and by such traditional texts (*smṛti*) as, "Brahman is neither suffering nor happiness, consisting of the past, the future, and the present. Therefore, reasoning (*tarka*) alone must be respected here; and since reasoning opposes the view that the Self has both the nature of consciousness and bliss, the scriptural mention of its being of the nature of bliss is merely figurative (*gauṇī*), intended to signify the cessation of suffering. Thus, the Self is of the nature of consciousness alone, like a person whose hand has been severed.
Just as no one would ever again grasp a severed hand, even so, one should not again identify with this body, senses, and so forth once they have been abandoned through discrimination (*viveka*).
Regarding the reality of the world:

in the world, it is observed that objects of dreams, such as the yellowness of a conch shell, are unreal because they are produced by an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) afflicted by defects such as sleep. However, because the *prakṛti* which is the cause of the expansion of the world beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), as well as the intellect (*buddhi*) of Hiraṇyagarbha, are not defective, the expansion of the world beginning with the Great Principle is not unreal.

Nor should it be argued that, because it is sublated by such scriptural passages as "There is no diversity here at all," some defect such as ignorance (avidyā) must be postulated; for the scripture "There is no diversity here" prohibits distinctions and the like according to its specific context, and does not intend to establish the absolute unreality of the phenomenal world (prapañca). Otherwise, the scripture itself would be sublated, resulting in the undesirable consequence that it could not establish its own meaning. For when a word used during a dream is sublated, the object indicated by it is not thereby rendered doubtful.

Therefore, based on the scriptural text "neither manifoldness nor non-manifoldness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19), the meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever distinct from Brahman. The Smṛti text as well—"You pervade all, therefore You are everything"—conveys this very same meaning. Furthermore, based on such scriptural texts as, "There is no destruction and no origination; no one is bound and no one is a seeker; no one desires liberation and no one is liberated—this is the ultimate truth," the meaning is the absence of any supreme ontological reality in the form of immutable permanence apart from the Self. Likewise, the meaning is simply that there is no destruction and so forth of the Self. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the teaching that such knowledge results in the fruit of liberation.
Birth is simply the transition of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) into a gross body (sthūladeha). The individual soul (jīva)—
The self characterized by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the individual soul (jīva).
One who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) becomes so precisely in the state of intermediate discernment. And it has been said:
"By the power of former practice, neither worldly nor Vedic action remains for him;
free from merit and demerit, the universal self—he is called one liberated while living. Thus it is said.
Knowledge— this refers to number and discriminative knowledge, which is the cause of liberation.
The organs of perception are five, known as the eye, ear, skin, tongue, and nose.

Contentment (*tuṣṭi*) is of nine kinds. Among these, there are four internal contentments known as *prakṛti*, *upādāna*, *kāla*, and *bhāgya*. In that regard, the contentment which arises from the view that "even the direct realization of discriminative discernment (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*) is merely a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); therefore, enough with the practice of meditation" and which consists in desisting from meditation and so forth, is called the contentment named *prakṛti*. This very one is termed "water" (*abbhas*). The contentment which holds that "liberation will come through the mere adoption of the life of a wandering mendicant (*pravrajyā*); what is the use of meditation and the like? is called the contentment named *upādāna*.

Its technical Tantric designation is "Salila. The contentment that thinks, "Even for one who has renounced worldly life, liberation will occur in due time; enough with this agitation," is called Kālākhyā (named Time), and is referred to as "Ogha" or "Megha. Similarly, the contentment based on fallacious reasoning which holds that "liberation will come through destiny alone, and not by the means prescribed in the scriptures on liberation," is called Bhāgyākhyā (named Destiny), and is referred to as "Vṛṣṭi."

Furthermore, there are five external contentments (*tuṣṭi*). These arise from the cessation of effort caused by perceiving the defects—such as acquisition, preservation, loss, enjoyment, and injury—in relation to the five external objects, beginning with sound. Their technical names, in order, are: *pāra*, *supāra*, *pārapāra*, *anuttamāmbhas*, and *uttamāmbhas*. Thus, all the contentments combined amount to nine. *Taijasa* means *rājasa* (the ego).

Direction (dik) is of two kinds: eternal and fragmentary. Among these, the eternal is merely a specific quality of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), whereas the fragmentary arises from space (*ākāśa*) through conjunction with its limiting adjuncts. The perceived means (dṛṣṭa-upāya) for the cessation of suffering are as follows: the consumption of medicine; the acquisition of desirable women, drinks, food, ointments, clothing, ornaments, and so forth; proficiency in the study of the treatises on ethics (*nīti-śāstra*); residence in a secure place free from danger; and the employment of gems, mantras, and the like. These are the perceived means for the removal of the threefold suffering. The cessation of suffering alone is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

Just as a person’s aversion toward suffering is more powerful than their desire for pleasure—which is, by comparison, weak—so too, even while subduing the desire for pleasure, the aversion toward suffering generates the very wish for the cessation of suffering. Furthermore, because suffering is more abundant than pleasure, it is established that the cessation of suffering alone is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). The fourfold classification of bodies: [The text continues with: *svedaja* (sweat-born), *jarāyuja* (womb-born), *aṇḍaja* (egg-born), and *udbhijja* (sprout-born). Among these, the *udbhijja* are further divided into two types: those that sprout from the earth and those that sprout from water. The *jarāyuja* are humans and certain animals. The *aṇḍaja* are birds and certain aquatic creatures. The *svedaja* are insects, moths, and the like. These are the four kinds of bodies. Among them, the *udbhijja* are considered the lowest, the *aṇḍaja* are superior to them, the *jarāyuja* are superior to those, and the *svedaja* are superior to those. Among all these, the human body is the most excellent. Why? Because it is the means for attaining liberation (*mokṣa*). It is said: "Among all bodies, the human body is the best, for it is through this that one attains the supreme state. Thus, the human body is the primary instrument for the attainment of the highest good. Therefore, the cessation of suffering is indeed the ultimate human goal. This concludes the section on the fourfold classification of bodies. Now, the definition of the three types of suffering: *ādhibhautika* (caused by other beings), *ādhidaivika* (caused by divine or natural forces), and *ādhyātmika* (internal). Among these, the *ādhibhautika* consists of suffering caused by humans, animals, and so forth. The *ādhidaivika* consists of suffering caused by cold, heat, wind, rain, and the like. The *ādhyātmika* is twofold: physical and mental. The physical arises from the imbalance of the bodily humors (*doṣas*), while the mental arises from passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). All these sufferings are to be avoided. Since they are undesirable, they must be abandoned. And since they are produced by causes, they can be brought to an end by removing those causes. Therefore, the cessation of suffering is possible. This is the meaning of the statement: "The cessation of suffering is the human goal. Thus, the purpose of the treatise is established. This concludes the introduction. Now, the definition of the three types of bodies: *sthūla* (gross), *liṅga* (subtle), and *kāraṇa* (causal). Among these, the *sthūla* body is composed of the five gross elements and is perceptible by the senses. The *liṅga* body is composed of the subtle elements and is imperceptible. The *kāraṇa* body is the primordial matter (*prakṛti*) itself. Among these, the *sthūla* body is the locus of experience, the *liṅga* body is the agent of experience, and the *kāraṇa* body is the cause of both. This concludes the section on the three types of bodies. Now, the definition of the three types of worlds: *bhūrloka*, *bhuvarloka*, and *svarloka*. Among these, *bhūrloka* extends from the surface of the earth up to the sun. *Bhuvarloka* extends from the sun up to the pole star (*dhruva*). *Svarloka* extends from the pole star up to the world of Brahmā. Beyond *svarloka* lies *maharloka*, *janaloka*, *tapoloka*, and *satyaloka*. These seven worlds constitute the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). This concludes the section on the three types of worlds. Now, the definition of the three types of time: past, present, and future. Among these, the past is that which has ceased, the present is that which exists, and the future is that which will come into being. Time is eternal and all-pervading. It is the cause of the manifestation and dissolution of all things. This concludes the section on the three types of time. Now, the definition of the three types of states: waking (*jāgrat*), dreaming (*svapna*), and deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Among these, the waking state is characterized by the perception of external objects through the senses. The dreaming state is characterized by the perception of internal objects through the mind. The deep sleep state is characterized by the absence of both external and internal perceptions, where the self rests in its own nature. This concludes the section on the three types of states. Now, the definition of the three types of selves: the *viśeṣa-ātman* (the individual self), the *sāmānya-ātman* (the universal self), and the *paramātman* (the supreme self). Among these, the *viśeṣa-ātman* is the embodied soul subject to transmigration. The *sāmānya-ātman* is the pure consciousness common to all individuals. The *paramātman* is the absolute reality, free from all attributes. This concludes the section on the three types of selves. Now, the definition of the three types of knowledge: *parokṣa* (indirect), *aparokṣa* (direct), and *tattvajñāna* (knowledge of reality). Among these, *parokṣa* is knowledge derived from inference or scripture. *Aparokṣa* is direct perception. *Tattvajñāna* is the knowledge of the principles as they truly are. This concludes the section on the three types of knowledge. Now, the definition of the three types of liberation: *kaivalya* (isolation), *sāyujya* (union), and *sālokya* (residence in the same world). Among these, *kaivalya* is the state of the self remaining in its own nature after the cessation of all adjuncts. *Sāyujya* is the merging of the individual self with the supreme self. *Sālokya* is the attainment of the same realm as the deity. This concludes the section on the three types of liberation. Now, the definition of the three types of means: *jñāna* (knowledge), *karma* (action), and *upāsanā* (devotion). Among these, *jñāna* is the means for attaining *kaivalya*. *Karma* is the means for attaining *sāyujya*. *Upāsanā* is the means for attaining *sālokya*. This concludes the section on the three types of means. Now, the definition of the three types of fruits: *anubhava* (experience), *prāpti* (attainment), and *pariṇāma* (transformation). Among these, *anubhava* is the direct experience of the fruit. *Prāpti* is the reaching of the fruit. *Pariṇāma* is the transformation of the fruit into another form. This concludes the section on the three types of fruits. Now, the definition of the three types of obstacles: *ādhyātmika* (internal), *ādhibhautika* (external), and *ādhidaivika* (supernatural). Among these, the *ādhyātmika* consists of diseases and mental afflictions. The *ādhibhautika* consists of dangers from humans and animals. The *ādhidaivika* consists of calamities such as lightning and thunder. These are the obstacles to the attainment of the human goal. This concludes the section on the three types of obstacles. Now, the definition of the three types of remedies: *pratisedha* (prohibition), *parihara* (avoidance), and *sādhana* (application of means). Among these, *pratisedha* is the avoidance of prohibited actions. *Parihara* is the removal of obstacles. *Sādhana* is the practice of prescribed means. This concludes the section on the three types of remedies. Now, the definition of the three types of results: *siddhi* (accomplishment), *niṣpatti* (completion), and *phalaprāpti* (attainment of the fruit). Among these, *siddhi* is the mastery of the means. *Niṣpatti* is the completion of the action. *Phalaprāpti* is the final attainment of the desired result. This concludes the section on the three types of results. Now, the definition of the three types of authorities: *śabda* (word/scripture), *anumāna* (inference),

There are four kinds of bodies: the body of action (*karmadeha*), the body of enjoyment (*upabhogadeha*), the body of both (*ubhayadeha*), and the body of dispassion (*viraktadeha*). Among these, the *karmadeha* belongs to those free from passion, who perform actions through the renunciation of fruits. The *upabhogadeha* belongs to animals and the like. The *karmopabhogadeha* (body of action and enjoyment) belongs to those entitled to ritual action who possess enjoyments, such as royal sages and others. The *anadhikārideha* (body of non-qualification) belongs to those who are dispassionate, such as Dattātreya, Jaḍabharata, and others. Aversion (*dveṣa*) is that which lies latent within suffering; according to its etymological derivation (*duḥkhamanuśete*), it arises immediately following suffering.
Dharma is that which is the effect of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose essence is unsurpassed goodness (*sattva*).

Dhāraṇā is the restraint and mastery of the vital breath through the processes of inhalation (*pūraka*), exhalation (*recaka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*). Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya-sūtra states: "Restraint [of the breath] occurs through vomiting and holding.
Dhyāna is meditation that destroys attachment to sense objects. Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya-sūtra states: "Dhyāna is the destruction of passion."

*dhvāntam*—darkness, which is *tamas*. And this is neither the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of light, nor its destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), nor its absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), nor its mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*); rather, it is a real entity distinct from non-existence. Furthermore, whether this is a quality (*guṇa*) or a substance (*dravya*) does not undermine the Sāṃkhya tenet, because the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the categories of existence are not fixed. Vijñānabhikṣu, however, asserts that the Sāṃkhya system does not accept such a doctrine of indeterminate categories.

Like a dancer: just as a dancer who has set out to perform for an audience ceases her dancing once it is completed, even so, when the purpose consisting in the attainment of the goal of the Puruṣa has been fulfilled, the Pradhāna also ceases.
"Destruction" (nāśa) means dissolution into the cause, that is to say, disappearance; thus says the Sāṃkhya-sūtra: "Destruction is dissolution into the cause.
"Naturally liberated" (nijamukta) means liberated by its very nature.

"Detached" (*niḥsaṅga*) means devoid of that conjunction which serves as the cause for [worldly] office (*adhikāra*). By this, although there exists a general conjunction due to [the soul's] omnipresence (*vibhutva*), there is no loss of detachment for the *puruṣa*, because the specific conjunction that causes office is absent.
"Eternally conscious" (*nityabuddha*) means having consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*citsvabhāva*), that is to say, eternal sentience (*nityacaitanya*).

Regarding the absence of eternal cognition and so forth: in the Sāṃkhya system, eternal knowledge, will, and action do not exist. For this very reason, there is no Lord (*īśvara*) whatsoever who could serve as a substratum for eternal cognition and the rest.
Eternally liberated—always free from bondage;
eternally pure—never touched by even a trace of modification;
absence of eternal connection—

There is no eternal relation whatsoever, because such a relation would have to be either conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*). It cannot be the former: since conjunction is produced by action, and action is absent in eternal and all-pervading entities, conjunction is impossible there; and even though conjunction exists among non-eternal things, that conjunction itself is non-eternal.

If it is argued: "Granted that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) may not be eternal, but let inherence (*samavāya*) be an eternal relation," we say no. If inherence itself were unconnected, it would be impossible for the two related entities to be connected to one another. If it is connected, by what relation is inherence connected? Since no other relation is possible, it must be said that it is connected by inherence itself.

If that were the case, there would be another inherence for that [inherence], and yet another for that one as well, resulting in the fallacy of infinite regress; thus, inherence itself remains unestablished. To avoid the fault of infinite regress, if the relatedness (or distinctness) of inherence were accepted as being by its very nature (*svarūpeṇa*), then the cognition of the distinctness of qualities and so forth should likewise be accepted as being by their very nature; what then is the use of inherence?

Nor should it be argued that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would likewise fail to be established as a relation because the cognition of a jar on the ground is accounted for by its own nature alone; for even at the time of disjunction, since the pot and the jujube fruit exist in their own nature, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a qualified cognition [of them as conjoined]. In the case of inherence (*samavāya*), however, that which is inherent is never separated from its own substratum; thus, if one accepts an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*) in that case, this fault does not arise. Therefore, the Sāṃkhya position is that inherence is not a relation at all. As in the case of the word "lotus-born" (*paṅkaja*).

Just as a lotus, though born from mud, does not retain the nature of mud, even so self-knowledge or liberation, though produced through the cooperation of worldly activity (*pravṛtti*), does not retain the nature of *saṃsāra*.
The five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell.

Pañcaśikha was a disciple of the sage Āsuri and a grand-disciple of the sage Kapila. In this regard, the authority is the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*: "The Sage [Kapila] gave this purifying and supreme [knowledge] to Āsuri out of compassion; Āsuri gave it to Pañcaśikha, and by him the system (*tantra*) was made manifold.
The practice of the five fires (*pañcāgniyoga*).
There is a connection with the pentad consisting of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, man, and woman as forms of fire;
there is no fixed rule regarding the number of categories.

The Vaiśeṣikas indeed maintain that there are six categories of existence, beginning with substance (dravya), while the Naiyāyikas maintain sixteen categories, beginning with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), the objects of cognition (prameya), doubt (saṃśaya), and purpose (prayojana). Both of these schools maintain that liberation arises from the knowledge of the true nature of those categories. However, in the Sāṃkhya system, which asserts an indefinite number of categories, there is no fixed limit to the number of categories; nor does liberation arise from the knowledge of those categories, since liberation is accepted as resulting solely from the knowledge of the Self (ātman).
The state of atoms having parts (*paramāṇu-sāvayavatvam*):

The Sāṃkhya position is that the partlessness of atoms as accepted by the Naiyāyikas and others does not exist, because they are effects (*kāryatvāt*). For this very reason, Vācaspatimiśra demonstrated in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya* that the subtle substances called *tanmātras* are indeed the constituent parts of the atoms of earth and the other elements.
The two-fold nature of dimension (*parimāṇa-dvaividhyam*):

In the Sāṃkhya system, there are only two types of dimension (*parimāṇa*): great (*mahat*) and minute (*aṇu*). All other specific dimensions are merely subdivisions of these two. Among them, short and long are simply intermediate subdivisions of great dimension; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite number of dimensions due to forms such as curved and so forth.
"Like a beast" (*paśuvat*):

just as a beast becomes subject to bondage and liberation through being smeared by a rope, in the very same way, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) alone—being smeared by states such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth—becomes subject to bondage and liberation, and not the *puruṣa*.
*pāñcabhautikaḥ*— the view of some is that the body is a transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the five elements combined together;
[this is] like Piṅgalā.

Just as the courtesan named Piṅgalā, who was seeking a lover and became miserable when she did not find one, became happy upon abandoning her hope; in the same way, a person should become happy through contentment by abandoning hope. As it has been said: "Hope is indeed the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness; just as Piṅgalā slept happily after completely severing her hope for a lover."

Like a *piśāca*: just as when Śrī Kṛṣṇa was imparting instruction on reality (*tattva*) for the sake of Arjuna, the *piśāca* standing nearby also attained discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), so too, having heard the instruction on reality being given to the Brāhmaṇa, women, *śūdras*, and others would also become knowers of reality.
A person (*pumān*):
the conscious individual (*puruṣa*) who is distinct from the body and other such [constituents].

The Puruṣa is uncomposite, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), immutable (kūṭastha), the seer, the enjoyer, all-pervading, eternal, and of the nature of consciousness; it is distinct in each body. Puruṣa, Ātman, Puman, Pudgala-jantu, Jīva, and Kṣetrajña are its synonyms.
As before—

*Pūrvavat* inference is that which has as its object a class (*jāti*) that has been previously perceived. For example, the inference of fire from smoke. Indeed, a member of the class "fire" was previously perceived in a kitchen (*mahānasa*) and so forth. Vācaspatimiśra, however, maintains: *Pūrvavat* is that which has as its object a universal (*sāmānya*) whose particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has been seen. For instance, when fire-ness as a specific universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) is inferred on a mountain from smoke, the particular characteristic of that fire-ness as a specific universal—the specific fire itself—was seen in the kitchen (*rasavati*). [The property of] being produced by a person (*pauruṣeyatva*)—

Whether an object has been seen or not seen, that object regarding which the cognition "it was made" arises is considered *pauruṣeya* (of human origin). According to the Sāṃkhya view, however, being *pauruṣeya* does not consist merely in being uttered by a person; for if it were so, even the Vedas would incur the status of being *pauruṣeya*, since they too were uttered by the Primordial Person (*ādipuruṣa*). Aniruddha also says: "That regarding which the cognition 'it was made' arises, even though it was not seen [being made], is *pauruṣeya*. On this view, it is not every effect (*kārya*) that implies an agent, but rather a specific kind of effect. — *Prakṛti* —

Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, or the triad of *sattva* and the others as characterized by that state of equilibrium. This state of equilibrium is a lack of combination due to the absence of deficiency or excess; the meaning is that it is a non-effectual state. Thus, it is concluded that Prakṛti is the three *guṇas* in a state distinct from their effects. And this is the definition of the Root-Prakṛti (*mūlaprakṛti*). However, the general definition of Prakṛti is: "The nature of being a Prakṛti is the state of being the material cause (*upādāna*) of another principle (*tattva*). [Objection: Obstruction—

Inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is pervasion (*vyāpti*). And that [pervasion] consists in the necessary coexistence of a fixed property (*niyatadharma*), or the coexistence with a property that constitutes the probandum (*sādhyātman*), between two properties that have equal pervasion—such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*)—or with a property that has unequal pervasion, such as smoke. Regarding this coexistence, the Commentator (*vṛttikāra*), by showing respect through the use of the term "the Teachers" (*ācāryāḥ*) in the Sūtra, states the Sāṃkhya view that it is the innate, inherent power (*nijā sahajā śaktiḥ*) of fire and smoke. "Bound" (*pratibaddha*) means the pervader, which is the probandum.
The non-discrimination of Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) alone is the cause for the non-discrimination of everything.

The *pradhāna* is the root of all things. From its non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the non-discrimination of other things arises. Whether there is non-discrimination or discrimination among individual objects, neither bondage nor liberation results from that; rather, they result from the non-discrimination or discrimination of the *pradhāna*. Therefore, when the non-discrimination of the *pradhāna* is abandoned, the abandonment of all non-discrimination occurs. This is the proof (*pramā*).

Valid cognition (*pramā*) is the spiritual awareness produced by a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*)—whether mediated through the channels of the senses and so forth or occurring directly—which has for its object a thing not yet known. Accordingly, the Sāṃkhya Sūtra states: "Valid cognition is the determination of an object not in contact [with the knower], whether for both [the internal organ and the self] or for either one of them. Here, "not in contact" means that the object has not yet ascended into the knower, that is to say, it is unapprehended. The determination or ascertainment of such an object—that is, a real entity—is valid cognition.

On this point, the author of the *Vṛtti* states that in the Sūtra, the word "of the two" (*dvayoḥ*) means "of the sense-organ and the object when both are present," with reference to perception (*pratyakṣa*). Likewise, he says that the word "of one or the other" (*ekatarasya*) means "of the present [probans]," whether referring to inference (*anumāna*) or verbal testimony (*śabda*). Vācaspatimiśra also says: "From the etymology 'that by which something is correctly known' (*pramīyate*), it is understood that [the instrument] is the means (*karaṇa*) for valid cognition (*pramā*). And that is a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) whose object is free from doubt, error, and non-apprehension; while the resulting human awareness is the fruit, which is the valid cognition (*pramā*). Thus ends the section on the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That which is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) toward a valid cognition (*pramā*) consisting of a human awareness (*pauruṣeyabodharūpā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). It should be understood that the determination (*paricchitti*) of an object not [otherwise] proximate (*asaṃnikṛṣṭārtha*)—whether belonging to both [the subject and the self] or to either one—is valid cognition (*pramā*); that which is the most effective instrument for that is the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, according to the *Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī*, the result (*phala*) is the valid cognition consisting of a human awareness, and the means of that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). On this view, the human awareness is the valid cognition (*pramā*), and the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) which serves as its cause is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

But when it is the mental modification itself, bearing the form of the object, that is designated by the term "valid cognition" (*pramā*), then it should be understood that its causes—the contact of the sense organs with their objects and so forth—are what are conventionally referred to as the "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*). As for the object of cognition (*prameya*)—

Those things which have become objects of valid cognition (*pramā*) are designated by the term "objects of knowledge" (*prameya*). The objects of knowledge accepted by the Sāṃkhya school are: primordial matter (*pradhāna*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), the five subtle elements (*pañcatanmātra*), the eleven organs (*ekādaśendriya*), the five gross elements (*pañcamahābhūta*), and the spirit (*puruṣa*). These twenty-five principles (*tattva*) are called the "manifest, the unmanifest, and the knower. Vijñānabhikṣu maintains that even the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), as the twenty-sixth object of knowledge, is included within the category of the *puruṣa* itself. Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)—

"A cognition that, being connected [with its object], reflects its form is perception (*pratyakṣa*)," according to the *Sāṃkhya-sūtra*. The *Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya* explains the essential point as follows: "Being connected, the cognition—which is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*)—assumes the form of the connected object; this is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception. Furthermore, the *Sāṃkhyakārikā* states: "Perception (*dṛṣṭa*) is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of each respective object."

Regarding this, the Gauḍapāda-bhāṣya states: "In each respective object—meaning the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the ears and other senses toward their objects such as sound—is 'seen' (*dṛṣṭa*), which is to say, perception (*pratyakṣa*). Vācaspatimiśra, however, explains: "That which operates toward each respective object (*viṣayaṃ viṣayaṃ prati vartate*) is the sense-organ (*indriya*), termed *prativiṣaya*. And 'operation' (*vṛtti*) means contact; thus, 'in contact with the object' (*arthasannikṛṣṭa*) is the meaning. Determination (*adhyavasāya*) is that which rests upon that [contact]; and determination is the activity of the intellect (*buddhi*), namely, cognition (*jñāna*)."

When there is contact (*saṃnikarṣa*)—that is, the functioning (*vṛtti*)—of the sense organs with their respective objects, and when darkness (*tamas*) is overcome, that which is the predominance of *sattva* is designated as "ascertainment" (*adhyavasāya*), "functioning" (*vṛtti*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*). This, first of all, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) known as perception (*pratyakṣa*). And this definition of perception is intended with reference to external perception; for the perception of yogis, however, is not external, and therefore it is not its object, nor does it depend upon contact with the sense organs.

Alternatively, even in the absence of sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣa*), the cognition of a yogin is brought into contact with objects solely through the assistance of the excellence produced by the dharma born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*); it also assumes the form of the object. Thus, the general definition of perception stated in the Sūtra—consisting of the grasping of the object's form by means of sensory contact—is indeed applicable to yogic perception as well. However, the requirement for sensory contact pertains only to specific types of perception, such as visual perception and the like.

One should not suspect that the aforementioned definition lacks applicability (*avyāpti*) to the eternal perception of God (*īśvara-pratyakṣa*), which is entirely independent of sensory contact (*sannikarṣa*), because there is no proof for the existence of God. Vijñānabhikṣu maintains that this response is intended according to the view of the *ekadeśins* (partial adherents). According to their method, the definition common to the perception of God is simply "being of the same class as knowledge produced by sensory contact," which is what the author of the Sūtras intended to express. Regarding the absence of dependence on form (*rūpa*) in perception:

The Sāṃkhya school, refuting the nihilistic (nāstika) position that "the direct perception of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is impossible because color (*rūpa*) is a cause for the direct perception of substances," does not accept the restrictive rule that color is a necessary condition for the perception of substances. Therefore, it holds that manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the manifester only with respect to the ordinary, external perception of substances.
[This is illustrated by] the serpent [perceived as such] once the reality of the rope has been awakened.

Just as for a person who has awakened to the true nature of the rope, the serpent no longer produces fear and so forth, whereas for the deluded person it certainly does; likewise, even though the *pradhāna* has become dispassionate toward one *puruṣa* following the realization of its distinctness from him, it does not become dispassionate toward other *puruṣas* for the sake of ceasing creation, but rather continues to create for them.
The distinction between the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) and the elemental air (*bhautikavāyu*):

The elemental air (*bhautika-vāyu*) that serves as the instrumental cause for the formation of the body is not the vital breath (*prāṇa-vāyu*). Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "The vital breath does not belong to that which initiates the body, because its establishment [as such] is due to the power of the sense organs.
*Prāṇādi* refers to the specific types of air beginning with *prāṇa*; there are five: *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *udāna*, *vyāna*, and *samāna*.

The sense organs function by reaching their objects—the sense organs do not illuminate what they have not reached, but rather only that which they have reached; that is to say, the sense organs illuminate only those objects with which they are in contact. By this much, the Sāṃkhya tenet is established that the sense organ is distinct from the physical orb (golaka).
Bondage—

Transmigration. And that bondage is threefold: natural (*prākṛtika*), modified (*vaikṛtika*), and personal (*dākṣiṇaka*). Among these, for those who worship Nature (*prakṛti*) because they lack knowledge of the Self, there is natural bondage. This very thing is called the bondage of those who are merged in Nature (*prakṛtilaya*). The second is modified bondage, belonging to those who worship the transformations themselves—the elements, the senses, ego, and intellect—mistaking them for the Puruṣa. Those who possess this bondage are called the "bodiless ones" (*videha*).

The southern bond (*dākṣiṇaka-bandha*) consists of *iṣṭāpūrta*—namely, sacrifice such as the *agnihotra*, as well as the construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and so forth. For one who performs *iṣṭāpūrta* without knowing the principle of the Puruṣa, being possessed by desire, becomes bound.
The external instruments (*bāhyakaraṇa*) consist of ten types: the five organs of cognition and the five organs of action.

*Buddhi* is the *mahat-tattva*. "The Great One" (*mahān*) is also a technical term for *buddhi* itself according to the Tantras. Regarding "the state of being Brahman": according to the Sūtra, "In samādhi, deep sleep, and liberation, there is the state of being Brahman," this refers to that which occurs when, in these states, due to the dissolution of *buddhi*, the limitations imposed by the adjunct of *buddhi* disappear, and the *puruṣas* abide in their own primordial nature. This very state is "the state of being Brahman. It is just as, when a jar is destroyed, the space within the jar attains its fullness.

And thus, such Brahmanhood itself is the very nature of persons, which, as has been stated, becomes manifest in their respective states. In this scripture, the word *brahman* denotes the universal consciousness that is free from limitations imposed by adjuncts (*upādhi*), impurity, and the like—so says Vijñānabhikṣu.
Aniruddha, however, [states]:

In this context, "being of the nature of Brahman" (brahmarūpatā) is intended as mere similarity to Brahman; and this similarity consists simply in the non-perception of external objects. This is because the non-perception of external objects is common to all three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep]. However, the actual, ontological nature of Brahman—consisting in the non-perception of suffering—is not what is intended here, because such a state is absent in both deep sleep and meditative absorption (samādhi).
The distinction here is as follows:

in both meditative absorption and deep sleep, there exists a "seeded" (sabījā) nature of Brahman, meaning it possesses latent impressions (saṃskāras) that serve as the cause for the recurrence of suffering. In liberation (mokṣa), however, there is a "seedless" (nirbījā) nature of Brahman, meaning it is devoid of such latent impressions.
Like Bharata—

just as for the royal sage Bharata, even the righteous nourishing of a helpless fawn resulted in bondage, so too for one possessed of discernment, the contemplation of improper means leads to bondage.
Regarding the creation of mental states (bhāvasarga):
The creation consists of eight states: dharma and adharma, knowledge and ignorance, detachment and non-detachment, and power and lack of power.

Like a servant—just as for an excellent servant, service to the master proceeds necessarily and by its very nature, not with the intention of self-enjoyment—so too the activity of *prakṛti* occurs by its very nature.
The absence of consciousness in the elements:

since consciousness is not observed in each individual element at the time of their division, it cannot emerge even in the state of their aggregation. Where a small power exists, a great power arises from its collection, as is seen in the case where the power to bind an elephant is observed to arise from a collection of threads possessing only slight power. However, such a separate consciousness is not observed in the elements such that consciousness could emerge upon their aggregation.
Therefore, the established conclusion is that consciousness does not exist within the elements, but rather there exists a conscious being entirely distinct from them.
"Element" (*bhūta*) refers to the fivefold elements: ether, air, fire, water, and earth.
"Origin of the elements" (*bhūtādi*) refers to the *ahaṅkāra* characterized by *tamas*.

"Like the female frog"—this illustrates through the example of the *bheki* (female frog) that even for a yogi, harm arises from forgetting a rule prescribed by the scriptures; what need is there to mention the transgression of a rule? A certain king, having gone hunting in the forest, saw a beautiful maiden. The king requested her hand in marriage. Having been thus requested, she made a condition: "Whenever you show me water, I shall depart from here."

Once, exhausted from playing, she asked the king, "Where is the water? The king, forgetting the agreement he had made, showed her the water; thereupon, that daughter of the frog-king, capable of assuming any form at will, turned into a frog and entered the water. Then the king, though searching with nets and other means, did not find her. In this very way, misfortune arises for a yogin when he forgets his own discipline (*niyama*). [The word] *bhoga*— [Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence. The term *bhoga* likely introduces a further illustration or explanation regarding the consequences of attachment.]

The enjoyment of objects (*viṣayabhoga*). This means ingestion, that is to say, making [the object] one's own (*ātmasātkaraṇa*). And the making of an object one's own for the *puruṣa* is merely a reflection [of it] within the *puruṣa*, because the *puruṣa* is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). However, for the body and so forth—which are distinct from the *puruṣa*—enjoyment consists of nourishment and the like, as well as the assuming of form, because they are changing (*pariṇāmin*). Thus, enjoyment is common to all things from the body up to consciousness (*cetanā*).

In some contexts, the prohibition of experience (*bhoga*) for the *puruṣa* refers only to that which consists of transformation (*pariṇāma*), and not to that which consists of the reception of a reflection (*pratibimba*). In reality, however, experience in the form of the fruit resides in the *puruṣa* alone, and not in the intellect (*buddhi*) or other faculties; for we observe the desire, "May I enjoy happiness. Therefore, the primary established doctrine is that pleasure, pain, and so forth are attributes of the intellect, while their experience belongs to the *puruṣa*.

The elemental creation (*bhautika-sarga*)—the creation of individual living beings (*bhūta*). It is threefold: the divine creation (*daiva-sarga*), the animal creation (*tairyagyona-sarga*), and the human creation (*mānuṣya-sarga*). Among these, the divine creation is of eight kinds: that of the Brahmas, Prajāpatis, Indras, Pitṛs, Gandharvas, Rākṣasas, and Piśācas. The human creation, however, is of only one kind, because the physical form is the same among all men. This has been stated in the *Sāṃkhyakārikā*:
The divine creation is of eight kinds, that of the animal realm is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; such, in brief, is the elemental creation. This is the intermediate discernment.

Following the direct realization of the Self (*ātma-sākṣātkāra*) through the yoga of occasional conscious concentration (*saṃprajñāta-yoga*), there occurs the intermediate state of discrimination (*madhya-viveka*). At that time, although suffering and other afflictions have been sublated, experience (*bhoga*) still occurs due to the persistence of their reflected forms within the Puruṣa by virtue of *prārabdha* karma. Furthermore, the perfection of discrimination occurs only through complete non-conceptual concentration (*asaṃprajñāta*); when that is present, there is no experience. Thus, the classification of discrimination consists of weak discrimination, intermediate discrimination, and the perfection of discrimination. The mind (*manas*) is of intermediate magnitude—

The all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the mind is refuted by the inference: "The mind is not all-pervasive, because it is an instrument, like speech and so forth. Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning the mind's departure to other worlds (*lokāntara*) also contradict its all-pervasiveness; for if the mind were all-pervasive, such departure to another world would be impossible, since it would already exist in that other world by virtue of being all-pervasive. Nor is the mind atomic (*aṇu*), because it cannot simultaneously engage with multiple sense organs. However, the fact that cognition and other functions pervade the body is accounted for by the mind possessing a medium-sized dimension.
And this is stated with reference to the mind (*manas*) in its state as an effect; however, in its causal state, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is indeed atomic (*aṇu*).
The "intermediate" one—the person (*puruṣa*)—is indifferent (*udāsīna*), being devoid of pleasure and pain.

An object that has been indistinctly perceived by a sense organ as "this is such-and-such" is properly conceptualized by the mind as "it is thus" or "it is not thus," and is discriminated according to the relationship between qualifier and qualified.
